title: Handling Difficult Customers
blurb: How to stay calm with angry or rude guests, find a solution, escalate, and step away if it turns threatening.
siteNotes: Who the duty manager is on each shift and how to call them quickly
What a front-line team member is allowed to offer to put things right
legalNotes: No legal rules in this trainer; it is service good practice.

cards.kicker: Front of house, bar and management · 10 minutes
cards.title: Handling Difficult Customers
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- stay calm and listen to an upset guest
- focus on what you can do, and escalate when needed
- know when to get a manager and step away

cards.title: Do not take it personally
cards.body: Now and then you will meet a guest who is angry, rude or hard to please. It is part of the job. Handled well, a difficult moment can turn a situation around. The wrong response makes it spiral.

items.title: Not personal
items.text: It is about the problem, not you.

cards.title: Calm is contagious
cards.body:
Calm is contagious, and so is anger. Keep your voice steady and low, keep your body language open and non-confrontational, and let the guest have their say without interrupting. Very often people just want to feel heard.

> "I can see why that's frustrating."

cards.title: Focus on what you CAN do
cards.body: Offer a solution where you are able to. If it is beyond your authority, do not dig in. Escalate to a manager. Knowing your limits is not failure; it is the right move. Never argue to win, because winning an argument with a guest usually loses the guest.

items.title: Escalate to a manager
items.text: If it is beyond your authority.

cards.title: You do not have to take abuse
cards.body: If a guest becomes abusive, threatening or aggressive, you do not have to stand there and take it. Staying calm, listening and knowing when to escalate keeps both you and the situation safe.

left.title: Do
items: Remove yourself from danger if needed

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Stay calm and do not take it personally
- Let them be heard, then acknowledge how they feel
- Offer what you can do; escalate what you cannot
- Never argue to win
- If abusive or threatening: get a manager, do not retaliate, step away

cards.q: With a difficult guest, the first rule is to stay calm and not take it personally.
cards.why: Staying calm is the first rule, and calm is contagious.

cards.q: Your voice and body language should be…
options: Light and joking to ease the mood
Quiet and turned away from them
Firm and loud so they know you mean it
Calm and non-confrontational
cards.why: Keep your voice steady and low and your body language open and non-confrontational.

cards.q: What do many angry guests simply want?
options: To feel heard
To speak to the owner
An apology in writing
A free meal
cards.why: Very often people just want to feel heard, so let them have their say without interrupting.

cards.q: You should focus on what you CAN do rather than what you cannot.
cards.why: Offer a solution where you are able to.

cards.q: If it is beyond your authority, you should…
options: Argue harder to hold your position
Escalate to a manager
Promise what they ask and sort it later
Ignore the guest until they leave
cards.why: Do not dig in. Bringing in a manager is exactly the right move.

cards.q: Winning an argument with a guest usually loses the guest.
cards.why: Never argue to win. Stay calm, listen and look for what you can do instead.

cards.q: What should you do if a guest becomes abusive or threatening?
options: Raise your voice so others notice
Ask the guest to leave without telling anyone
Stand your ground until they calm down
Get a manager, do not retaliate, and step away if in danger
cards.why: You do not have to stand there and take it. Get a manager, do not retaliate, and remove yourself from danger if you need to.

cards.q: You have to stand and take it if a guest is aggressive.
cards.why: There is a firm line: abuse, threats and aggression do not have to be tolerated.

cards.q: Acknowledging a guest's feelings helps to…
options: Hand the problem to someone else
Make the problem seem bigger
Calm things down
Prove that they are wrong
cards.why: A line like "I can see why that's frustrating" shows you want to help and calms things down.

cards.q: Knowing your limits and asking for help is the right move, not a failure.
cards.why: Escalating to a manager is exactly the right move.
